To share a slab across threads, it may be wrapped in an `Arc`:

```
use std::sync::Arc;
let slab = Arc::new(Slab::new());
let slab2 = slab.clone();
let thread2 = std::thread::spawn(move || {
    let key = slab2.insert("hello from thread two").unwrap();
    assert_eq!(slab2.get(key).unwrap(), "hello from thread two");
    key
});
let key1 = slab.insert("hello from thread one").unwrap();
assert_eq!(slab.get(key1).unwrap(), "hello from thread one");
// Wait for thread 2 to complete.
let key2 = thread2.join().unwrap();
// The item inserted by thread 2 remains in the slab.
assert_eq!(slab.get(key2).unwrap(), "hello from thread two");
```
If items in the slab must be mutated, a `Mutex` or `RwLock` may be used for
each item, providing granular locking of items rather than of the slab:

```
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
let slab = Arc::new(Slab::new());
let key = slab.insert(Mutex::new(String::from("hello world"))).unwrap();
let slab2 = slab.clone();
let thread2 = std::thread::spawn(move || {
    let hello = slab2.get(key).expect("item missing");
    let mut hello = hello.lock().expect("mutex poisoned");
    *hello = String::from("hello everyone!");
});
thread2.join().unwrap();
let hello = slab.get(key).expect("item missing");
let mut hello = hello.lock().expect("mutex poisoned");
assert_eq!(hello.as_str(), "hello everyone!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#configuration)Configuration

For performance reasons, several values used by the slab are calculated as
constants. In order to allow users to tune the slab’s parameters, we provide
a [ Config](https://docs.rs/trait.Config.html) trait which defines these parameters as associated

`consts`.
The `Slab` type is generic over a `C: Config` parameter.[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-with-similar-crates)Comparison with Similar Crates

-
`slab``slab`crate provides a slab implementation with a similar API, implemented by storing all data in a single vector.Unlike `sharded_slab`, inserting and removing elements from the slab requires mutable access. This means that if the slab is accessed concurrently by multiple threads, it is necessary for it to be protected by a`Mutex`or`RwLock`. Items may not be inserted or removed (or accessed, if a`Mutex`is used) concurrently, even when they are unrelated. In many cases, the lock can become a significant bottleneck. On the other hand, this crate allows separate indices in the slab to be accessed, inserted, and removed concurrently without requiring a global lock. Therefore, when the slab is shared across multiple threads, this crate offers significantly better performance than`slab`.However, the lock free slab introduces some additional constant-factor overhead. This means that in use-cases where a slab is *not*shared by multiple threads and locking is not required, this crate will likely offer slightly worse performance.In summary: `sharded-slab`offers significantly improved performance in concurrent use-cases, while`slab`should be preferred in single-threaded use-cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-and-correctness)Safety and Correctness

Most implementations of lock-free data structures in Rust require some
amount of unsafe code, and this crate is not an exception. In order to catch
potential bugs in this unsafe code, we make use of [ loom](https://crates.io/crates/loom), a
permutation-testing tool for concurrent Rust programs. All

`unsafe` blocks
this crate occur in accesses to `loom` `UnsafeCell`s. This means that when
those accesses occur in this crate’s tests, `loom` will assert that they are
valid under the C11 memory model across multiple permutations of concurrent
executions of those tests.In order to guard against the [ABA problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABA_problem), this crate makes use of
*generational indices*. Each slot in the slab tracks a generation counter
which is incremented every time a value is inserted into that slot, and the
indices returned by [ Slab::insert](https://docs.rs/struct.Slab.html#method.insert) include the generation of the slot when
the value was inserted, packed into the high-order bits of the index. This
ensures that if a value is inserted, removed,  and a new value is inserted
into the same slot in the slab, the key returned by the first call to

`insert` will not map to the new value.Since a fixed number of bits are set aside to use for storing the generation counter, the counter will wrap around after being incremented a number of times. To avoid situations where a returned index lives long enough to see the generation counter wrap around to the same value, it is good to be fairly generous when configuring the allocation of index bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

These graphs were produced by [benchmarks](https://github.com/hawkw/sharded-slab/blob/master/benches/bench.rs) of the sharded slab implementation,
using the [ criterion](https://crates.io/crates/criterion) crate.

The first shows the results of a benchmark where an increasing number of
items are inserted and then removed into a slab concurrently by five
threads. It compares the performance of the sharded slab implementation
with a `RwLock<slab::Slab>`:

The second graph shows the results of a benchmark where an increasing
number of items are inserted and then removed by a *single* thread. It
compares the performance of the sharded slab implementation with an
`RwLock<slab::Slab>` and a `mut slab::Slab`.

These benchmarks demonstrate that, while the sharded approach introduces a small constant-factor overhead, it offers significantly better performance across concurrent accesses.

# lib.rs - source

# sharded_slab/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A lock-free concurrent slab.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! Slabs provide pre-allocated storage for many instances of a single data
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! type. When a large number of values of a single type are required,
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! this can be more efficient than allocating each item individually. Since the
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! allocated items are the same size, memory fragmentation is reduced, and
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! creating and removing new items can be very cheap.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! This crate implements a lock-free concurrent slab, indexed by `usize`s.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! ## Usage
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! First, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! ```toml
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! sharded-slab = "0.1.1"
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! ```
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! This crate provides two  types, [`Slab`] and [`Pool`], which provide
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! slightly different APIs for using a sharded slab.
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! [`Slab`] implements a slab for _storing_ small types, sharing them between
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! threads, and accessing them by index. New entries are allocated by
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! [inserting] data, moving it in by value. Similarly, entries may be
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! deallocated by [taking] from the slab, moving the value out. This API is
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! similar to a `Vec<Option<T>>`, but allowing lock-free concurrent insertion
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! and removal.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! In contrast, the [`Pool`] type provides an [object pool] style API for
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! _reusing storage_. Rather than constructing values and moving them into the
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! pool, as with [`Slab`], [allocating an entry][create] from the pool takes a
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! closure that's provided with a mutable reference to initialize the entry in
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! place. When entries are deallocated, they are [cleared] in place. Types
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! which own a heap allocation can be cleared by dropping any _data_ they
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! store, but retaining any previously-allocated capacity. This means that a
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! [`Pool`] may be used to reuse a set of existing heap allocations, reducing
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! allocator load.
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! [inserting]: Slab::insert
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! [taking]: Slab::take
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! [create]: Pool::create
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! [cleared]: Clear
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! [object pool]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_pool_pattern
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! # Examples
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! Inserting an item into the slab, returning an index:
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! ```rust
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! let slab = Slab::new();
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! assert_eq!(slab.get(key).unwrap(), "hello world");
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! ```
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! To share a slab across threads, it may be wrapped in an `Arc`:
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ```rust
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! use std::sync::Arc;
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! let slab = Arc::new(Slab::new());
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! let slab2 = slab.clone();
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! let thread2 = std::thread::spawn(move || {
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!     let key = slab2.insert("hello from thread two").unwrap();
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!     assert_eq!(slab2.get(key).unwrap(), "hello from thread two");
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!     key
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! });
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! let key1 = slab.insert("hello from thread one").unwrap();
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! assert_eq!(slab.get(key1).unwrap(), "hello from thread one");
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! // Wait for thread 2 to complete.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! let key2 = thread2.join().unwrap();
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! // The item inserted by thread 2 remains in the slab.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! assert_eq!(slab.get(key2).unwrap(), "hello from thread two");
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!```
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! If items in the slab must be mutated, a `Mutex` or `RwLock` may be used for
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! each item, providing granular locking of items rather than of the slab:
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! ```rust
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! let slab = Arc::new(Slab::new());
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! let key = slab.insert(Mutex::new(String::from("hello world"))).unwrap();
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! let slab2 = slab.clone();
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! let thread2 = std::thread::spawn(move || {
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     let hello = slab2.get(key).expect("item missing");
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     let mut hello = hello.lock().expect("mutex poisoned");
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!     *hello = String::from("hello everyone!");
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! });
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! thread2.join().unwrap();
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! let hello = slab.get(key).expect("item missing");
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! let mut hello = hello.lock().expect("mutex poisoned");
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! assert_eq!(hello.as_str(), "hello everyone!");
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! ```

[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!   use-cases.

[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! # Safety and Correctness
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! Most implementations of lock-free data structures in Rust require some
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! amount of unsafe code, and this crate is not an exception. In order to catch
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! potential bugs in this unsafe code, we make use of [`loom`], a
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! permutation-testing tool for concurrent Rust programs. All `unsafe` blocks
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! this crate occur in accesses to `loom` `UnsafeCell`s. This means that when
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! those accesses occur in this crate's tests, `loom` will assert that they are
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! valid under the C11 memory model across multiple permutations of concurrent
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! executions of those tests.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! In order to guard against the [ABA problem][aba], this crate makes use of
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! _generational indices_. Each slot in the slab tracks a generation counter
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! which is incremented every time a value is inserted into that slot, and the
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! indices returned by [`Slab::insert`] include the generation of the slot when
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! the value was inserted, packed into the high-order bits of the index. This
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! ensures that if a value is inserted, removed,  and a new value is inserted
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! into the same slot in the slab, the key returned by the first call to
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! `insert` will not map to the new value.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! Since a fixed number of bits are set aside to use for storing the generation
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! counter, the counter will wrap  around after being incremented a number of
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! times. To avoid situations where a returned index lives long enough to see the
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! generation counter wrap around to the same value, it is good to be fairly
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! generous when configuring the allocation of index bits.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! [`loom`]: https://crates.io/crates/loom
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! [aba]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABA_problem
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! [`Slab::insert`]: struct.Slab.html#method.insert

[240](https://docs.rs#240)/// A handle that allows access to an occupied entry in a [`Slab`].
[241](https://docs.rs#241)///
[242](https://docs.rs#242)/// While the guard exists, it indicates to the slab that the item the guard
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// references is currently being accessed. If the item is removed from the slab
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// while a guard exists, the removal will be deferred until all guards are
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// dropped.
[246](https://docs.rs#246)pub struct Entry<'a, T, C: cfg::Config = DefaultConfig> {
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    inner: page::slot::Guard<Option<T>, C>,
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    value: ptr::NonNull<T>,
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    shard: &'a Shard<Option<T>, C>,
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    key: usize,
[251](https://docs.rs#251)}
[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// A handle to a vacant entry in a [`Slab`].
[254](https://docs.rs#254)///
[255](https://docs.rs#255)/// `VacantEntry` allows constructing values with the key that they will be
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// assigned to.
[257](https://docs.rs#257)///
[258](https://docs.rs#258)/// # Examples
[259](https://docs.rs#259)///
[260](https://docs.rs#260)/// ```
[261](https://docs.rs#261)/// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[262](https://docs.rs#262)/// let mut slab = Slab::new();
[263](https://docs.rs#263)///
[264](https://docs.rs#264)/// let hello = {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)///     let entry = slab.vacant_entry().unwrap();
[266](https://docs.rs#266)///     let key = entry.key();
[267](https://docs.rs#267)///
[268](https://docs.rs#268)///     entry.insert((key, "hello"));
[269](https://docs.rs#269)///     key
[270](https://docs.rs#270)/// };
[271](https://docs.rs#271)///
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// assert_eq!(hello, slab.get(hello).unwrap().0);
[273](https://docs.rs#273)/// assert_eq!("hello", slab.get(hello).unwrap().1);
[274](https://docs.rs#274)/// ```
[275](https://docs.rs#275)#[derive(Debug)]
[276](https://docs.rs#276)pub struct VacantEntry<'a, T, C: cfg::Config = DefaultConfig> {
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    inner: page::slot::InitGuard<Option<T>, C>,
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    key: usize,
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    _lt: PhantomData<&'a ()>,
[280](https://docs.rs#280)}
[281](https://docs.rs#281)
[282](https://docs.rs#282)/// An owned reference to an occupied entry in a [`Slab`].
[283](https://docs.rs#283)///
[284](https://docs.rs#284)/// While the guard exists, it indicates to the slab that the item the guard
[285](https://docs.rs#285)/// references is currently being accessed. If the item is removed from the slab
[286](https://docs.rs#286)/// while the guard exists, the  removal will be deferred until all guards are
[287](https://docs.rs#287)/// dropped.
[288](https://docs.rs#288)///
[289](https://docs.rs#289)/// Unlike [`Entry`], which borrows the slab, an `OwnedEntry` clones the [`Arc`]
[290](https://docs.rs#290)/// around the slab. Therefore, it keeps the slab from being dropped until all
[291](https://docs.rs#291)/// such guards have been dropped. This means that an `OwnedEntry` may be held for
[292](https://docs.rs#292)/// an arbitrary lifetime.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// # Examples
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// ```
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// use std::sync::Arc;
[299](https://docs.rs#299)///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());
[301](https://docs.rs#301)/// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[302](https://docs.rs#302)///
[303](https://docs.rs#303)/// // Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// let value = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
[305](https://docs.rs#305)///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)/// // Now, the original `Arc` clone of the slab may be dropped, but the
[307](https://docs.rs#307)/// // returned `OwnedEntry` can still access the value.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)/// assert_eq!(value, "hello world");
[309](https://docs.rs#309)/// ```
[310](https://docs.rs#310)///
[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// Unlike [`Entry`], an `OwnedEntry` may be stored in a struct which must live
[312](https://docs.rs#312)/// for the `'static` lifetime:
[313](https://docs.rs#313)///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)/// ```
[315](https://docs.rs#315)/// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// use sharded_slab::OwnedEntry;
[317](https://docs.rs#317)/// use std::sync::Arc;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)///
[319](https://docs.rs#319)/// pub struct MyStruct {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)///     entry: OwnedEntry<&'static str>,
[321](https://docs.rs#321)///     // ... other fields ...
[322](https://docs.rs#322)/// }
[323](https://docs.rs#323)///
[324](https://docs.rs#324)/// // Suppose this is some arbitrary function which requires a value that
[325](https://docs.rs#325)/// // lives for the 'static lifetime...
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// fn function_requiring_static<T: 'static>(t: &T) {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)///     // ... do something extremely important and interesting ...
[328](https://docs.rs#328)/// }
[329](https://docs.rs#329)///
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());
[331](https://docs.rs#331)/// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[332](https://docs.rs#332)///
[333](https://docs.rs#333)/// // Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// let entry = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
[335](https://docs.rs#335)/// let my_struct = MyStruct {
[336](https://docs.rs#336)///     entry,
[337](https://docs.rs#337)///     // ...
[338](https://docs.rs#338)/// };
[339](https://docs.rs#339)///
[340](https://docs.rs#340)/// // We can use `my_struct` anywhere where it is required to have the
[341](https://docs.rs#341)/// // `'static` lifetime:
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// function_requiring_static(&my_struct);
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// ```
[344](https://docs.rs#344)///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// `OwnedEntry`s may be sent between threads:
[346](https://docs.rs#346)///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)/// ```
[348](https://docs.rs#348)/// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// use std::{thread, sync::Arc};
[350](https://docs.rs#350)///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());
[352](https://docs.rs#352)/// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[353](https://docs.rs#353)///
[354](https://docs.rs#354)/// // Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// let value = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
[356](https://docs.rs#356)///
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// thread::spawn(move || {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)///     assert_eq!(value, "hello world");
[359](https://docs.rs#359)///     // ...
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// }).join().unwrap();
[361](https://docs.rs#361)/// ```
[362](https://docs.rs#362)///
[363](https://docs.rs#363)/// [`get`]: Slab::get
[364](https://docs.rs#364)/// [`Arc`]: std::sync::Arc
[365](https://docs.rs#365)pub struct OwnedEntry<T, C = DefaultConfig>
[366](https://docs.rs#366)where
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    C: cfg::Config,
[368](https://docs.rs#368){
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    inner: page::slot::Guard<Option<T>, C>,
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    value: ptr::NonNull<T>,
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    slab: Arc<Slab<T, C>>,
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    key: usize,
[373](https://docs.rs#373)}
[374](https://docs.rs#374)

[379](https://docs.rs#379)    }
[380](https://docs.rs#380)
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// Returns a new slab with the provided configuration parameters.
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    pub fn new_with_config<C: cfg::Config>() -> Slab<T, C> {
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        C::validate();
[384](https://docs.rs#384)        Slab {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)            shards: shard::Array::new(),
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            _cfg: PhantomData,

[390](https://docs.rs#390)
[391](https://docs.rs#391)impl<T, C: cfg::Config> Slab<T, C> {
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// The number of bits in each index which are used by the slab.
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    ///
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// If other data is packed into the `usize` indices returned by
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    /// [`Slab::insert`], user code is free to use any bits higher than the
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// `USED_BITS`-th bit freely.
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// This is determined by the [`Config`] type that configures the slab's
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// parameters. By default, all bits are used; this can be changed by
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// overriding the [`Config::RESERVED_BITS`][res] constant.
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    ///
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// [res]: crate::Config#RESERVED_BITS
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    pub const USED_BITS: usize = C::USED_BITS;
[404](https://docs.rs#404)
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// Inserts a value into the slab, returning the integer index at which that
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// value was inserted. This index can then be used to access the entry.
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    ///
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// If this function returns `None`, then the shard for the current thread
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// is full and no items can be added until some are removed, or the maximum
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// number of shards has been reached.
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// # Examples
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// ```rust
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// let slab = Slab::new();
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    ///
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// assert_eq!(slab.get(key).unwrap(), "hello world");
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// ```
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    pub fn insert(&self, value: T) -> Option<usize> {
[421](https://docs.rs#421)        let (tid, shard) = self.shards.current();
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        test_println!("insert {:?}", tid);
[423](https://docs.rs#423)        let mut value = Some(value);
[424](https://docs.rs#424)        shard
[425](https://docs.rs#425)            .init_with(|idx, slot| {
[426](https://docs.rs#426)                let gen = slot.insert(&mut value)?;
[427](https://docs.rs#427)                Some(gen.pack(idx))
[428](https://docs.rs#428)            })
[429](https://docs.rs#429)            .map(|idx| tid.pack(idx))
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    }
[431](https://docs.rs#431)
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// Return a handle to a vacant entry allowing for further manipulation.
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    ///
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// This function is useful when creating values that must contain their
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// slab index. The returned [`VacantEntry`] reserves a slot in the slab and
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// is able to return the index of the entry.
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    ///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// # Examples
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    ///
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// ```
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    /// let mut slab = Slab::new();
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    ///
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// let hello = {
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    ///     let entry = slab.vacant_entry().unwrap();
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    ///     let key = entry.key();
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    ///
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    ///     entry.insert((key, "hello"));
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    ///     key
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    /// };
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    ///
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    /// assert_eq!(hello, slab.get(hello).unwrap().0);
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    /// assert_eq!("hello", slab.get(hello).unwrap().1);
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// ```
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    pub fn vacant_entry(&self) -> Option<VacantEntry<'_, T, C>> {
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        let (tid, shard) = self.shards.current();
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        test_println!("vacant_entry {:?}", tid);
[458](https://docs.rs#458)        shard.init_with(|idx, slot| {
[459](https://docs.rs#459)            let inner = slot.init()?;
[460](https://docs.rs#460)            let key = inner.generation().pack(tid.pack(idx));
[461](https://docs.rs#461)            Some(VacantEntry {
[462](https://docs.rs#462)                inner,
[463](https://docs.rs#463)                key,
[464](https://docs.rs#464)                _lt: PhantomData,
[465](https://docs.rs#465)            })
[466](https://docs.rs#466)        })
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    }
[468](https://docs.rs#468)
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// Remove the value at the given index in the slab, returning `true` if a
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    /// value was removed.
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    ///
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    /// Unlike [`take`], this method does _not_ block the current thread until
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    /// the value can be removed. Instead, if another thread is currently
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    /// accessing that value, this marks it to be removed by that thread when it
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    /// finishes accessing the value.
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    ///
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    /// # Examples
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    ///
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    /// ```rust
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    /// let slab = sharded_slab::Slab::new();
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    ///
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    /// // Remove the item from the slab.
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    /// assert!(slab.remove(key));
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    ///
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    /// // Now, the slot is empty.
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    /// assert!(!slab.contains(key));
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    /// ```
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    ///
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    /// ```rust
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    /// use std::sync::Arc;
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    ///
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    /// let slab = Arc::new(sharded_slab::Slab::new());
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    ///
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    /// let slab2 = slab.clone();
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    /// let thread2 = std::thread::spawn(move || {
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    ///     // Depending on when this thread begins executing, the item may
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    ///     // or may not have already been removed...
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    ///     if let Some(item) = slab2.get(key) {
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    ///         assert_eq!(item, "hello world");
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    ///     }
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    /// });
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    ///
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    /// // The item will be removed by thread2 when it finishes accessing it.
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    /// assert!(slab.remove(key));
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    ///
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    /// thread2.join().unwrap();
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    /// assert!(!slab.contains(key));
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    /// ```
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    /// [`take`]: Slab::take
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    pub fn remove(&self, idx: usize) -> bool {
[513](https://docs.rs#513)        // The `Drop` impl for `Entry` calls `remove_local` or `remove_remote` based
[514](https://docs.rs#514)        // on where the guard was dropped from. If the dropped guard was the last one, this will
[515](https://docs.rs#515)        // call `Slot::remove_value` which actually clears storage.
[516](https://docs.rs#516)        let tid = C::unpack_tid(idx);
[517](https://docs.rs#517)
[518](https://docs.rs#518)        test_println!("rm_deferred {:?}", tid);
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        let shard = self.shards.get(tid.as_usize());
[520](https://docs.rs#520)        if tid.is_current() {
[521](https://docs.rs#521)            shard.map(|shard| shard.remove_local(idx)).unwrap_or(false)
[522](https://docs.rs#522)        } else {
[523](https://docs.rs#523)            shard.map(|shard| shard.remove_remote(idx)).unwrap_or(false)
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        }
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    }
[526](https://docs.rs#526)
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    /// Removes the value associated with the given key from the slab, returning
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    /// it.
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    ///
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    /// If the slab does not contain a value for that key, `None` is returned
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    /// instead.
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    ///
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    /// If the value associated with the given key is currently being
[534](https://docs.rs#534)    /// accessed by another thread, this method will block the current thread
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    /// until the item is no longer accessed. If this is not desired, use
[536](https://docs.rs#536)    /// [`remove`] instead.
[537](https://docs.rs#537)    ///
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    /// **Note**: This method blocks the calling thread by spinning until the
[539](https://docs.rs#539)    /// currently outstanding references are released. Spinning for long periods
[540](https://docs.rs#540)    /// of time can result in high CPU time and power consumption. Therefore,
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    /// `take` should only be called when other references to the slot are
[542](https://docs.rs#542)    /// expected to be dropped soon (e.g., when all accesses are relatively
[543](https://docs.rs#543)    /// short).
[544](https://docs.rs#544)    ///
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    /// # Examples
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    ///
[547](https://docs.rs#547)    /// ```rust
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    /// let slab = sharded_slab::Slab::new();
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    ///
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    /// // Remove the item from the slab, returning it.
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    /// assert_eq!(slab.take(key), Some("hello world"));
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    ///
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    /// // Now, the slot is empty.
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    /// assert!(!slab.contains(key));
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    /// ```
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    ///
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    /// ```rust
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    /// use std::sync::Arc;
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    ///
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    /// let slab = Arc::new(sharded_slab::Slab::new());
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    ///
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    /// let slab2 = slab.clone();
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// let thread2 = std::thread::spawn(move || {
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    ///     // Depending on when this thread begins executing, the item may
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    ///     // or may not have already been removed...
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    ///     if let Some(item) = slab2.get(key) {
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    ///         assert_eq!(item, "hello world");
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    ///     }
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// });
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    ///
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    /// // The item will only be removed when the other thread finishes
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// // accessing it.
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    /// assert_eq!(slab.take(key), Some("hello world"));
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    ///
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    /// thread2.join().unwrap();
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    /// assert!(!slab.contains(key));
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    /// ```
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// [`remove`]: Slab::remove
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    pub fn take(&self, idx: usize) -> Option<T> {
[582](https://docs.rs#582)        let tid = C::unpack_tid(idx);
[583](https://docs.rs#583)
[584](https://docs.rs#584)        test_println!("rm {:?}", tid);
[585](https://docs.rs#585)        let shard = self.shards.get(tid.as_usize())?;
[586](https://docs.rs#586)        if tid.is_current() {
[587](https://docs.rs#587)            shard.take_local(idx)
[588](https://docs.rs#588)        } else {
[589](https://docs.rs#589)            shard.take_remote(idx)
[590](https://docs.rs#590)        }
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    }
[592](https://docs.rs#592)
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    /// Return a reference to the value associated with the given key.
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    ///
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    /// If the slab does not contain a value for the given key, or if the
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    /// maximum number of concurrent references to the slot has been reached,
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    /// `None` is returned instead.
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    ///
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    /// # Examples
[600](https://docs.rs#600)    ///
[601](https://docs.rs#601)    /// ```rust
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    /// let slab = sharded_slab::Slab::new();
[603](https://docs.rs#603)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    ///
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    /// assert_eq!(slab.get(key).unwrap(), "hello world");
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    /// assert!(slab.get(12345).is_none());
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    /// ```
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    pub fn get(&self, key: usize) -> Option<Entry<'_, T, C>> {
[609](https://docs.rs#609)        let tid = C::unpack_tid(key);
[610](https://docs.rs#610)
[611](https://docs.rs#611)        test_println!("get {:?}; current={:?}", tid, Tid::<C>::current());
[612](https://docs.rs#612)        let shard = self.shards.get(tid.as_usize())?;
[613](https://docs.rs#613)        shard.with_slot(key, |slot| {
[614](https://docs.rs#614)            let inner = slot.get(C::unpack_gen(key))?;
[615](https://docs.rs#615)            let value = ptr::NonNull::from(slot.value().as_ref().unwrap());
[616](https://docs.rs#616)            Some(Entry {
[617](https://docs.rs#617)                inner,
[618](https://docs.rs#618)                value,
[619](https://docs.rs#619)                shard,
[620](https://docs.rs#620)                key,
[621](https://docs.rs#621)            })
[622](https://docs.rs#622)        })
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    }
[624](https://docs.rs#624)
[625](https://docs.rs#625)    /// Return an owned reference to the value at the given index.
[626](https://docs.rs#626)    ///
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    /// If the slab does not contain a value for the given key, `None` is
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    /// returned instead.
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    ///
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    /// Unlike [`get`], which borrows the slab, this method _clones_ the [`Arc`]
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    /// around the slab. This means that the returned [`OwnedEntry`] can be held
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    /// for an arbitrary lifetime. However,  this method requires that the slab
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    /// itself be wrapped in an `Arc`.
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    ///
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    /// # Examples
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    ///
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    /// ```
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    /// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// use std::sync::Arc;
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    ///
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    ///
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    /// // Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// let value = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    ///
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    /// // Now, the original `Arc` clone of the slab may be dropped, but the
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    /// // returned `OwnedEntry` can still access the value.
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    /// assert_eq!(value, "hello world");
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    /// ```
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    ///
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    /// Unlike [`Entry`], an `OwnedEntry` may be stored in a struct which must live
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    /// for the `'static` lifetime:
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    ///
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    /// ```
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    /// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    /// use sharded_slab::OwnedEntry;
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    /// use std::sync::Arc;
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    ///
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    /// pub struct MyStruct {
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    ///     entry: OwnedEntry<&'static str>,
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    ///     // ... other fields ...
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    /// }
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    ///
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    /// // Suppose this is some arbitrary function which requires a value that
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    /// // lives for the 'static lifetime...
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    /// fn function_requiring_static<T: 'static>(t: &T) {
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    ///     // ... do something extremely important and interesting ...
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    /// }
[670](https://docs.rs#670)    ///
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    /// let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    ///
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    /// // Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    /// let entry = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    /// let my_struct = MyStruct {
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    ///     entry,
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    ///     // ...
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    /// };
[680](https://docs.rs#680)    ///
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    /// // We can use `my_struct` anywhere where it is required to have the
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    /// // `'static` lifetime:
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    /// function_requiring_static(&my_struct);
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    /// ```
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    ///
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// [`OwnedEntry`]s may be sent between threads:
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    ///
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    /// ```
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// use std::{thread, sync::Arc};
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    ///
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    /// let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    ///
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    /// // Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    /// let value = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    ///
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    /// thread::spawn(move || {
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    ///     assert_eq!(value, "hello world");
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    ///     // ...
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    /// }).join().unwrap();
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    /// ```
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    ///
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    /// [`get`]: Slab::get
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    /// [`Arc`]: std::sync::Arc
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    pub fn get_owned(self: Arc<Self>, key: usize) -> Option<OwnedEntry<T, C>> {
[707](https://docs.rs#707)        let tid = C::unpack_tid(key);
[708](https://docs.rs#708)
[709](https://docs.rs#709)        test_println!("get_owned {:?}; current={:?}", tid, Tid::<C>::current());
[710](https://docs.rs#710)        let shard = self.shards.get(tid.as_usize())?;
[711](https://docs.rs#711)        shard.with_slot(key, |slot| {
[712](https://docs.rs#712)            let inner = slot.get(C::unpack_gen(key))?;
[713](https://docs.rs#713)            let value = ptr::NonNull::from(slot.value().as_ref().unwrap());
[714](https://docs.rs#714)            Some(OwnedEntry {
[715](https://docs.rs#715)                inner,
[716](https://docs.rs#716)                value,
[717](https://docs.rs#717)                slab: self.clone(),
[718](https://docs.rs#718)                key,
[719](https://docs.rs#719)            })
[720](https://docs.rs#720)        })
[721](https://docs.rs#721)    }
[722](https://docs.rs#722)
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    /// Returns `true` if the slab contains a value for the given key.
[724](https://docs.rs#724)    ///
[725](https://docs.rs#725)    /// # Examples
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    ///
[727](https://docs.rs#727)    /// ```
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    /// let slab = sharded_slab::Slab::new();
[729](https://docs.rs#729)    ///
[730](https://docs.rs#730)    /// let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
[731](https://docs.rs#731)    /// assert!(slab.contains(key));
[732](https://docs.rs#732)    ///
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    /// slab.take(key).unwrap();
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    /// assert!(!slab.contains(key));
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    /// ```
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    pub fn contains(&self, key: usize) -> bool {
[737](https://docs.rs#737)        self.get(key).is_some()
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    }
[739](https://docs.rs#739)
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    /// Returns an iterator over all the items in the slab.
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    ///
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    /// Because this iterator exclusively borrows the slab (i.e. it holds an
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    /// `&mut Slab<T>`), elements will not be added or removed while the
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    /// iteration is in progress.
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    pub fn unique_iter(&mut self) -> iter::UniqueIter<'_, T, C> {
[746](https://docs.rs#746)        let mut shards = self.shards.iter_mut();
[747](https://docs.rs#747)
[748](https://docs.rs#748)        let (pages, slots) = match shards.next() {
[749](https://docs.rs#749)            Some(shard) => {
[750](https://docs.rs#750)                let mut pages = shard.iter();
[751](https://docs.rs#751)                let slots = pages.next().and_then(page::Shared::iter);
[752](https://docs.rs#752)                (pages, slots)
[753](https://docs.rs#753)            }
[754](https://docs.rs#754)            None => ([].iter(), None),
[755](https://docs.rs#755)        };
[756](https://docs.rs#756)
[757](https://docs.rs#757)        iter::UniqueIter {
[758](https://docs.rs#758)            shards,
[759](https://docs.rs#759)            pages,
[760](https://docs.rs#760)            slots,
[761](https://docs.rs#761)        }
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    }

[810](https://docs.rs#810)impl<'a, T, C: cfg::Config> Drop for Entry<'a, T, C> {
[811](https://docs.rs#811)    fn drop(&mut self) {
[812](https://docs.rs#812)        let should_remove = unsafe {
[813](https://docs.rs#813)            // Safety: calling `slot::Guard::release` is unsafe, since the
[814](https://docs.rs#814)            // `Guard` value contains a pointer to the slot that may outlive the
[815](https://docs.rs#815)            // slab containing that slot. Here, the `Entry` guard owns a
[816](https://docs.rs#816)            // borrowed reference to the shard containing that slot, which
[817](https://docs.rs#817)            // ensures that the slot will not be dropped while this `Guard`
[818](https://docs.rs#818)            // exists.
[819](https://docs.rs#819)            self.inner.release()
[820](https://docs.rs#820)        };
[821](https://docs.rs#821)        if should_remove {
[822](https://docs.rs#822)            self.shard.clear_after_release(self.key)
[823](https://docs.rs#823)        }
[824](https://docs.rs#824)    }

[849](https://docs.rs#849)impl<'a, T, C: cfg::Config> VacantEntry<'a, T, C> {
[850](https://docs.rs#850)    /// Insert a value in the entry.
[851](https://docs.rs#851)    ///
[852](https://docs.rs#852)    /// To get the integer index at which this value will be inserted, use
[853](https://docs.rs#853)    /// [`key`] prior to calling `insert`.
[854](https://docs.rs#854)    ///
[855](https://docs.rs#855)    /// # Examples
[856](https://docs.rs#856)    ///
[857](https://docs.rs#857)    /// ```
[858](https://docs.rs#858)    /// # use sharded_slab::Slab;
[859](https://docs.rs#859)    /// let mut slab = Slab::new();
[860](https://docs.rs#860)    ///
[861](https://docs.rs#861)    /// let hello = {
[862](https://docs.rs#862)    ///     let entry = slab.vacant_entry().unwrap();
[863](https://docs.rs#863)    ///     let key = entry.key();
[864](https://docs.rs#864)    ///
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    ///     entry.insert((key, "hello"));
[866](https://docs.rs#866)    ///     key
[867](https://docs.rs#867)    /// };
[868](https://docs.rs#868)    ///
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    /// assert_eq!(hello, slab.get(hello).unwrap().0);
[870](https://docs.rs#870)    /// assert_eq!("hello", slab.get(hello).unwrap().1);
[871](https://docs.rs#871)    /// ```
[872](https://docs.rs#872)    ///
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    /// [`key`]: VacantEntry::key
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    pub fn insert(mut self, val: T) {
[875](https://docs.rs#875)        let value = unsafe {
[876](https://docs.rs#876)            // Safety: this `VacantEntry` only lives as long as the `Slab` it was
[877](https://docs.rs#877)            // borrowed from, so it cannot outlive the entry's slot.
[878](https://docs.rs#878)            self.inner.value_mut()
[879](https://docs.rs#879)        };
[880](https://docs.rs#880)        debug_assert!(
[881](https://docs.rs#881)            value.is_none(),
[882](https://docs.rs#882)            "tried to insert to a slot that already had a value!"
[883](https://docs.rs#883)        );
[884](https://docs.rs#884)        *value = Some(val);
[885](https://docs.rs#885)        let _released = unsafe {
[886](https://docs.rs#886)            // Safety: again, this `VacantEntry` only lives as long as the
[887](https://docs.rs#887)            // `Slab` it was borrowed from, so it cannot outlive the entry's
[888](https://docs.rs#888)            // slot.
[889](https://docs.rs#889)            self.inner.release()
[890](https://docs.rs#890)        };
[891](https://docs.rs#891)        debug_assert!(
[892](https://docs.rs#892)            !_released,
[893](https://docs.rs#893)            "removing a value before it was inserted should be a no-op"
[894](https://docs.rs#894)        )
[895](https://docs.rs#895)    }
[896](https://docs.rs#896)
[897](https://docs.rs#897)    /// Return the integer index at which this entry will be inserted.
[898](https://docs.rs#898)    ///
[899](https://docs.rs#899)    /// A value stored in this entry will be associated with this key.
[900](https://docs.rs#900)    ///
[901](https://docs.rs#901)    /// # Examples
[902](https://docs.rs#902)    ///
[903](https://docs.rs#903)    /// ```
[904](https://docs.rs#904)    /// # use sharded_slab::*;
[905](https://docs.rs#905)    /// let mut slab = Slab::new();
[906](https://docs.rs#906)    ///
[907](https://docs.rs#907)    /// let hello = {
[908](https://docs.rs#908)    ///     let entry = slab.vacant_entry().unwrap();
[909](https://docs.rs#909)    ///     let key = entry.key();
[910](https://docs.rs#910)    ///
[911](https://docs.rs#911)    ///     entry.insert((key, "hello"));
[912](https://docs.rs#912)    ///     key
[913](https://docs.rs#913)    /// };
[914](https://docs.rs#914)    ///
[915](https://docs.rs#915)    /// assert_eq!(hello, slab.get(hello).unwrap().0);
[916](https://docs.rs#916)    /// assert_eq!("hello", slab.get(hello).unwrap().1);
[917](https://docs.rs#917)    /// ```
[918](https://docs.rs#918)    pub fn key(&self) -> usize {
[919](https://docs.rs#919)        self.key
[920](https://docs.rs#920)    }

[955](https://docs.rs#955)impl<T, C> Drop for OwnedEntry<T, C>
[956](https://docs.rs#956)where
[957](https://docs.rs#957)    C: cfg::Config,
[958](https://docs.rs#958){
[959](https://docs.rs#959)    fn drop(&mut self) {
[960](https://docs.rs#960)        test_println!("drop OwnedEntry: try clearing data");
[961](https://docs.rs#961)        let should_clear = unsafe {
[962](https://docs.rs#962)            // Safety: calling `slot::Guard::release` is unsafe, since the
[963](https://docs.rs#963)            // `Guard` value contains a pointer to the slot that may outlive the
[964](https://docs.rs#964)            // slab containing that slot. Here, the `OwnedEntry` owns an `Arc`
[965](https://docs.rs#965)            // clone of the pool, which keeps it alive as long as the `OwnedEntry`
[966](https://docs.rs#966)            // exists.
[967](https://docs.rs#967)            self.inner.release()
[968](https://docs.rs#968)        };
[969](https://docs.rs#969)        if should_clear {
[970](https://docs.rs#970)            let shard_idx = Tid::<C>::from_packed(self.key);
[971](https://docs.rs#971)            test_println!("-> shard={:?}", shard_idx);
[972](https://docs.rs#972)            if let Some(shard) = self.slab.shards.get(shard_idx.as_usize()) {
[973](https://docs.rs#973)                shard.clear_after_release(self.key)
[974](https://docs.rs#974)            } else {
[975](https://docs.rs#975)                test_println!("-> shard={:?} does not exist! THIS IS A BUG", shard_idx);
[976](https://docs.rs#976)                debug_assert!(std::thread::panicking(), "[internal error] tried to drop an `OwnedEntry` to a slot on a shard that never existed!");
[977](https://docs.rs#977)            }
[978](https://docs.rs#978)        }
[979](https://docs.rs#979)    }

# Pool in sharded_slab - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sharded-slab/0.1.7/sharded_slab/struct.Pool.html

`pub struct Pool<T, C = `[DefaultConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultConfig.html)>{ /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A lock-free concurrent object pool.

Slabs provide pre-allocated storage for many instances of a single type. But, when working with heap allocated objects, the advantages of a slab are lost, as the memory allocated for the object is freed when the object is removed from the slab. With a pool, we can instead reuse this memory for objects being added to the pool in the future, therefore reducing memory fragmentation and avoiding additional allocations.

This type implements a lock-free concurrent pool, indexed by `usize`s. The items stored in this
type need to implement [ Clear](https://docs.rs/trait.Clear.html) and

`Default`.The `Pool` type shares similar semantics to [ Slab](https://docs.rs/struct.Slab.html) when it comes to sharing across threads
and storing mutable shared data. The biggest difference is there are no

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Slab.html#method.insert)

`Slab::insert`[analouges for the](https://docs.rs/struct.Slab.html#method.take)

`Slab::take``Pool` type. Instead new items are added to the pool by using
the [method, and marked for clearing by the](https://docs.rs/struct.Pool.html#method.create)

`Pool::create`[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.Pool.html#method.clear)

`Pool::clear`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Add an entry to the pool, returning an index:

```
let pool: Pool<String> = Pool::new();
let key = pool.create_with(|item| item.push_str("hello world")).unwrap();
assert_eq!(pool.get(key).unwrap(), String::from("hello world"));
```
Create a new pooled item, returning a guard that allows mutable access:

```
let pool: Pool<String> = Pool::new();
let mut guard = pool.create().unwrap();
let key = guard.key();
guard.push_str("hello world");
drop(guard); // release the guard, allowing immutable access.
assert_eq!(pool.get(key).unwrap(), String::from("hello world"));
```
Pool entries can be cleared by calling [ Pool::clear](https://docs.rs/struct.Pool.html#method.clear). This marks the entry to
be cleared when the guards referencing to it are dropped.

```
let pool: Pool<String> = Pool::new();
let key = pool.create_with(|item| item.push_str("hello world")).unwrap();
// Mark this entry to be cleared.
pool.clear(key);
// The cleared entry is no longer available in the pool
assert!(pool.get(key).is_none());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#configuration)Configuration

Both `Pool` and [ Slab](https://docs.rs/struct.Slab.html) share the same configuration mechanism. See

[crate level documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html#configuration)for more details.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

The number of bits in each index which are used by the pool.

If other data is packed into the `usize` indices returned by
[ Pool::create](https://docs.rs/struct.Pool.html#method.create), user code is free to use any bits higher than the

`USED_BITS`-th bit freely.This is determined by the [ Config](https://docs.rs/trait.Config.html) type that configures the pool’s
parameters. By default, all bits are used; this can be changed by
overriding the

[constant.](https://docs.rs/trait.Config.html#associatedconstant.RESERVED_BITS)

`Config::RESERVED_BITS`Creates a new object in the pool, returning an [ RefMut](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.RefMut.html) guard that
may be used to mutate the new object.

If this function returns `None`, then the shard for the current thread is full and no items
can be added until some are removed, or the maximum number of shards has been reached.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
let pool: Pool<String> = Pool::new();
// Create a new pooled item, returning a guard that allows mutable
// access to the new item.
let mut item = pool.create().unwrap();
// Return a key that allows indexing the created item once the guard
// has been dropped.
let key = item.key();
// Mutate the item.
item.push_str("Hello");
// Drop the guard, releasing mutable access to the new item.
drop(item);
/// Other threads may now (immutably) access the item using the returned key.
thread::spawn(move || {
   assert_eq!(pool.get(key).unwrap(), String::from("Hello"));
}).join().unwrap();
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sharded_slab/pool.rs.html#619-632)#### pub fn [create_owned](https://docs.rs#method.create_owned)(self: [Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<Self>) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[OwnedRefMut](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.OwnedRefMut.html)<T, C>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sharded_slab/pool.rs.html#619-632)

#### pub fn [create_owned](https://docs.rs#method.create_owned)(self: [Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<Self>) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[OwnedRefMut](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.OwnedRefMut.html)<T, C>>

Creates a new object in the pool, returning an [ OwnedRefMut](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.OwnedRefMut.html) guard that
may be used to mutate the new object.

If this function returns `None`, then the shard for the current thread
is full and no items can be added until some are removed, or the maximum
number of shards has been reached.

Unlike [ create](https://docs.rs/struct.Pool.html#method.create), which borrows the pool, this method

*clones*the

`Arc`
around the pool if a value exists for the given key. This means that the
returned [can be held for an arbitrary lifetime. However, this method requires that the pool itself be wrapped in an](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.OwnedRefMut.html)

`OwnedRefMut``Arc`.An `OwnedRefMut<T>` functions more or less identically to an owned
`Box<T>`: it can be passed to functions, stored in structure fields, and
borrowed mutably or immutably, and can be owned for arbitrary lifetimes.
The difference is that, unlike a `Box<T>`, the memory allocation for the
`T` lives in the `Pool`; when an `OwnedRefMut` is created, it may reuse
memory that was allocated for a previous pooled object that has been
cleared. Additionally, the `OwnedRefMut` may be [downgraded](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.OwnedRefMut.html#method.downgrade) to an
[ OwnedRef](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.OwnedRef.html) which may be shared freely, essentially turning the

`Box`
into an `Arc`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use std::sync::Arc;
let pool: Arc<Pool<String>> = Arc::new(Pool::new());
// Create a new pooled item, returning an owned guard that allows mutable
// access to the new item.
let mut item = pool.clone().create_owned().unwrap();
// Return a key that allows indexing the created item once the guard
// has been dropped.
let key = item.key();
// Mutate the item.
item.push_str("Hello");
// Drop the guard, releasing mutable access to the new item.
drop(item);
/// Other threads may now (immutably) access the item using the returned key.
thread::spawn(move || {
   assert_eq!(pool.get(key).unwrap(), String::from("Hello"));
}).join().unwrap();
```
```
use std::sync::Arc;
let pool: Arc<Pool<String>> = Arc::new(Pool::new());
// Create a new item, returning an owned, mutable guard.
let mut value = pool.clone().create_owned().unwrap();
// Now, the original `Arc` clone of the pool may be dropped, but the
// returned `OwnedRefMut` can still access the value.
drop(pool);
value.push_str("hello world");
assert_eq!(value, String::from("hello world"));
```
Unlike [ RefMut](https://docs.rs/pool/struct.RefMut.html), an

`OwnedRefMut` may be stored in a struct which must live
for the `'static` lifetime:```
use sharded_slab::pool::OwnedRefMut;
use std::sync::Arc;
pub struct MyStruct {
    pool_ref: OwnedRefMut<String>,
    // ... other fields ...
}
// Suppose this is some arbitrary function which requires a value that
// lives for the 'static lifetime...
fn function_requiring_static<T: 'static>(t: &T) {
    // ... do something extremely important and interesting ...
}
let pool: Arc<Pool<String>> = Arc::new(Pool::new());
// Create a new item, returning a mutable owned reference.
let pool_ref = pool.clone().create_owned().unwrap();
let my_struct = MyStruct {
    pool_ref,
    // ...
};
// We can use `my_struct` anywhere where it is required to have the
// `'static` lifetime:
function_requiring_static(&my_struct);
```
`OwnedRefMut`s may be sent between threads:

```
use std::{thread, sync::Arc};
let pool: Arc<Pool<String>> = Arc::new(Pool::new());
let mut value = pool.clone().create_owned().unwrap();
let key = value.key();
thread::spawn(move || {
    value.push_str("hello world");
    // ...
}).join().unwrap();
// Once the `OwnedRefMut` has been dropped by the other thread, we may
// now access the value immutably on this thread.
assert_eq!(pool.get(key).unwrap(), String::from("hello world"));
```
Downgrading from a mutable to an immutable reference:

```
use std::{thread, sync::Arc};
let pool: Arc<Pool<String>> = Arc::new(Pool::new());
let mut value = pool.clone().create_owned().unwrap();
let key = value.key();
value.push_str("hello world");
// Downgrade the mutable owned ref to an immutable owned ref.
let value = value.downgrade();
// Once the `OwnedRefMut` has been downgraded, other threads may
// immutably access the pooled value:
thread::spawn(move || {
    assert_eq!(pool.get(key).unwrap(), String::from("hello world"));
}).join().unwrap();
// This thread can still access the pooled value through the
// immutable owned ref:
assert_eq!(value, String::from("hello world"));
```
Creates a new object in the pool with the provided initializer, returning a key that may be used to access the new object.

If this function returns `None`, then the shard for the current thread is full and no items
can be added until some are removed, or the maximum number of shards has been reached.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
let pool: Pool<String> = Pool::new();
// Create a new pooled item, returning its integer key.
let key = pool.create_with(|s| s.push_str("Hello")).unwrap();
/// Other threads may now (immutably) access the item using the key.
thread::spawn(move || {
   assert_eq!(pool.get(key).unwrap(), String::from("Hello"));
}).join().unwrap();
```
Return a borrowed reference to the value associated with the given key.

If the pool does not contain a value for the given key, `None` is returned instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
let pool: Pool<String> = Pool::new();
let key = pool.create_with(|item| item.push_str("hello world")).unwrap();

assert!(pool.get(12345).is_none());
```
Return an owned reference to the value associated with the given key.

If the pool does not contain a value for the given key, `None` is
returned instead.

`OwnedRef`s may be sent between threads:

Remove the value using the storage associated with the given key from the pool, returning
`true` if the value was removed.

This method does *not* block the current thread until the value can be
cleared. Instead, if another thread is currently accessing that value, this marks it to be
cleared by that thread when it is done accessing that value.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
let pool: Pool<String> = Pool::new();
// Check out an item from the pool.
let mut item = pool.create().unwrap();
let key = item.key();
item.push_str("hello world");
drop(item);
assert_eq!(pool.get(key).unwrap(), String::from("hello world"));
pool.clear(key);
assert!(pool.get(key).is_none());
```
```
let pool: Pool<String> = Pool::new();
let key = pool.create_with(|item| item.push_str("Hello world!")).unwrap();
// Clearing a key that doesn't exist in the `Pool` will return `false`
assert_eq!(pool.clear(key + 69420), false);
// Clearing a key that does exist returns `true`
assert!(pool.clear(key));
// Clearing a key that has previously been cleared will return `false`
assert_eq!(pool.clear(key), false);
```

#### pub fn [vacant_entry](https://docs.rs#method.vacant_entry)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[VacantEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.VacantEntry.html)<'_, T, C>>

Return a handle to a vacant entry allowing for further manipulation.

This function is useful when creating values that must contain their
slab index. The returned [ VacantEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.VacantEntry.html) reserves a slot in the slab and
is able to return the index of the entry.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
let mut slab = Slab::new();
let hello = {
    let entry = slab.vacant_entry().unwrap();
    let key = entry.key();
    entry.insert((key, "hello"));
    key
};
assert_eq!(hello, slab.get(hello).unwrap().0);
assert_eq!("hello", slab.get(hello).unwrap().1);
```
Remove the value at the given index in the slab, returning `true` if a
value was removed.

Unlike [ take](https://docs.rs/struct.Slab.html#method.take), this method does

*not*block the current thread until the value can be removed. Instead, if another thread is currently accessing that value, this marks it to be removed by that thread when it finishes accessing the value.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
let slab = sharded_slab::Slab::new();
let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
// Remove the item from the slab.
assert!(slab.remove(key));
// Now, the slot is empty.
assert!(!slab.contains(key));
```
```
use std::sync::Arc;
let slab = Arc::new(sharded_slab::Slab::new());
let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
let slab2 = slab.clone();
let thread2 = std::thread::spawn(move || {
    // Depending on when this thread begins executing, the item may
    // or may not have already been removed...
    if let Some(item) = slab2.get(key) {
        assert_eq!(item, "hello world");
    }
});
// The item will be removed by thread2 when it finishes accessing it.
assert!(slab.remove(key));
thread2.join().unwrap();
assert!(!slab.contains(key));
```
Removes the value associated with the given key from the slab, returning it.

If the slab does not contain a value for that key, `None` is returned
instead.

If the value associated with the given key is currently being
accessed by another thread, this method will block the current thread
until the item is no longer accessed. If this is not desired, use
[ remove](https://docs.rs/struct.Slab.html#method.remove) instead.

**Note**: This method blocks the calling thread by spinning until the
currently outstanding references are released. Spinning for long periods
of time can result in high CPU time and power consumption. Therefore,
`take` should only be called when other references to the slot are
expected to be dropped soon (e.g., when all accesses are relatively
short).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
let slab = sharded_slab::Slab::new();
let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
// Remove the item from the slab, returning it.
assert_eq!(slab.take(key), Some("hello world"));
// Now, the slot is empty.
assert!(!slab.contains(key));
```
```
use std::sync::Arc;
let slab = Arc::new(sharded_slab::Slab::new());
let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
let slab2 = slab.clone();
let thread2 = std::thread::spawn(move || {
    // Depending on when this thread begins executing, the item may
    // or may not have already been removed...
    if let Some(item) = slab2.get(key) {
        assert_eq!(item, "hello world");
    }
});
// The item will only be removed when the other thread finishes
// accessing it.
assert_eq!(slab.take(key), Some("hello world"));
thread2.join().unwrap();
assert!(!slab.contains(key));
```
Return a reference to the value associated with the given key.

If the slab does not contain a value for the given key, or if the
maximum number of concurrent references to the slot has been reached,
`None` is returned instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
let slab = sharded_slab::Slab::new();
let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
assert_eq!(slab.get(key).unwrap(), "hello world");
assert!(slab.get(12345).is_none());
```
Return an owned reference to the value at the given index.

If the slab does not contain a value for the given key, `None` is
returned instead.

Unlike [ get](https://docs.rs/struct.Slab.html#method.get), which borrows the slab, this method

*clones*the

[around the slab. This means that the returned](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)

`Arc`[can be held for an arbitrary lifetime. However, this method requires that the slab itself be wrapped in an](https://docs.rs/struct.OwnedEntry.html)

`OwnedEntry``Arc`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use std::sync::Arc;
let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());
let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
// Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
let value = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
// Now, the original `Arc` clone of the slab may be dropped, but the
// returned `OwnedEntry` can still access the value.

```
Unlike [ Entry](https://docs.rs/struct.Entry.html), an

`OwnedEntry` may be stored in a struct which must live
for the `'static` lifetime:```
use sharded_slab::OwnedEntry;
use std::sync::Arc;
pub struct MyStruct {
    entry: OwnedEntry<&'static str>,
    // ... other fields ...
}
// Suppose this is some arbitrary function which requires a value that
// lives for the 'static lifetime...
fn function_requiring_static<T: 'static>(t: &T) {
    // ... do something extremely important and interesting ...
}
let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());
let key = slab.insert("hello world").unwrap();
// Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
let entry = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
let my_struct = MyStruct {
    entry,
    // ...
};
// We can use `my_struct` anywhere where it is required to have the
// `'static` lifetime:
function_requiring_static(&my_struct);
```
[ OwnedEntry](https://docs.rs/struct.OwnedEntry.html)s may be sent between threads:

```
use std::{thread, sync::Arc};
let slab: Arc<Slab<&'static str>> = Arc::new(Slab::new());

// Look up the created key, returning an `OwnedEntry`.
let value = slab.clone().get_owned(key).unwrap();
thread::spawn(move || {
    assert_eq!(value, "hello world");
    // ...
}).join().unwrap();
```

    fn
```
[clear](https://docs.rs#tymethod.clear)(&mut self);
}## Expand description

Trait implemented by types which can be cleared in place, retaining any allocated memory.

This is essentially a generalization of methods on standard library
collection types, including as [ Vec::clear](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.clear),

[, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/string/struct.String.html#method.clear)

`String::clear`[. These methods drop all data stored in the collection, but retain the collection’s heap allocation for future use. Types such as](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html#method.clear)

`HashMap::clear``BTreeMap`, whose `clear` methods drops allocations, should not
implement this trait.When implemented for types which do not own a heap allocation, `Clear`
should reset the type in place if possible. If the type has an empty state
or stores `Option`s, those values should be reset to the empty state. For
“plain old data” types, which hold no pointers to other data and do not have
an empty or initial state, it’s okay for a `Clear` implementation to be a
no-op. In that case, it essentially serves as a marker indicating that the
type may be reused to store new data.

The maximum number of threads which can access the slab.

This value (rounded to a power of two) determines the number of shards in the slab. If a thread is created, accesses the slab, and then terminates, its shard may be reused and thus does not count against the maximum number of threads once the thread has terminated.

The maximum number of pages in each shard in the slab.

This value, in combination with `INITIAL_PAGE_SIZE`, determines how many
bits of each index are used to represent page addresses.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sharded_slab/cfg.rs.html#30)#### const [INITIAL_PAGE_SIZE](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.INITIAL_PAGE_SIZE): [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html) = DefaultConfig::INITIAL_PAGE_SIZE

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sharded_slab/cfg.rs.html#30)

#### const [INITIAL_PAGE_SIZE](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.INITIAL_PAGE_SIZE): [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html) = DefaultConfig::INITIAL_PAGE_SIZE

The size of the first page in each shard.

When a page in a shard has been filled with values, a new page will be allocated that is twice as large as the previous page. Thus, the second page will be twice this size, and the third will be four times this size, and so on.

Note that page sizes must be powers of two. If this value is not a power of two, it will be rounded to the next power of two.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sharded_slab/cfg.rs.html#39)#### const [RESERVED_BITS](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.RESERVED_BITS): [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html) = 0

#### const [RESERVED_BITS](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.RESERVED_BITS): [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html) = 0

Sets a number of high-order bits in each index which are reserved from user code.

Note that these bits are taken from the generation counter; if the page address and thread IDs are configured to use a large number of bits, reserving additional bits will decrease the period of the generation counter. These should thus be used relatively sparingly, to ensure that generation counters are able to effectively prevent the ABA problem.

# sharded_slab::implementation - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sharded-slab/0.1.7/sharded_slab/implementation/index.html

## Expand description

Notes on `sharded-slab`’s implementation and design.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

The sharded slab’s design is strongly inspired by the ideas presented by
Leijen, Zorn, and de Moura in [Mimalloc: Free List Sharding in
Action](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2019/06/mimalloc-tr-v1.pdf). In this report, the authors present a novel design for a
memory allocator based on a concept of *free list sharding*.

Memory allocators must keep track of what memory regions are not currently
allocated (“free”) in order to provide them to future allocation requests.
The term [ free list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_list) refers to a technique for performing this
bookkeeping, where each free block stores a pointer to the next free block,
forming a linked list. The memory allocator keeps a pointer to the most
recently freed block, the

*head*of the free list. To allocate more memory, the allocator pops from the free list by setting the head pointer to the next free block of the current head block, and returning the previous head. To deallocate a block, the block is pushed to the free list by setting its first word to the current head pointer, and the head pointer is set to point to the deallocated block. Most implementations of slab allocators backed by arrays or vectors use a similar technique, where pointers are replaced by indices into the backing array.

When allocations and deallocations can occur concurrently across threads,
they must synchronize accesses to the free list; either by putting the
entire allocator state inside of a lock, or by using atomic operations to
treat the free list as a lock-free structure (such as a [Treiber stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treiber_stack)). In
both cases, there is a significant performance cost — even when the free
list is lock-free, it is likely that a noticeable amount of time will be
spent in compare-and-swap loops. Ideally, the global synchronzation point
created by the single global free list could be avoided as much as possible.

The approach presented by Leijen, Zorn, and de Moura is to introduce
sharding and thus increase the granularity of synchronization significantly.
In mimalloc, the heap is *sharded* so that each thread has its own
thread-local heap. Objects are always allocated from the local heap of the
thread where the allocation is performed. Because allocations are always
done from a thread’s local heap, they need not be synchronized.

However, since objects can move between threads before being deallocated,
*deallocations* may still occur concurrently. Therefore, Leijen et al.
introduce a concept of *local* and *global* free lists. When an object is
deallocated on the same thread it was originally allocated on, it is placed
on the local free list; if it is deallocated on another thread, it goes on
the global free list for the heap of the thread from which it originated. To
allocate, the local free list is used first; if it is empty, the entire
global free list is popped onto the local free list. Since the local free
list is only ever accessed by the thread it belongs to, it does not require
synchronization at all, and because the global free list is popped from
infrequently, the cost of synchronization has a reduced impact. A majority
of allocations can occur without any synchronization at all; and
deallocations only require synchronization when an object has left its
parent thread (a relatively uncommon case).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

A slab is represented as an array of `MAX_THREADS`*shards*. A shard
consists of a vector of one or more *pages* plus associated metadata.
Finally, a page consists of an array of *slots*, head indices for the local
and remote free lists.

```
┌─────────────┐
│ shard 1     │
│             │    ┌─────────────┐        ┌────────┐
│ pages───────┼───▶│ page 1      │        │        │
├─────────────┤    ├─────────────┤  ┌────▶│  next──┼─┐
│ shard 2     │    │ page 2      │  │     ├────────┤ │
├─────────────┤    │             │  │     │XXXXXXXX│ │
│ shard 3     │    │ local_head──┼──┘     ├────────┤ │
└─────────────┘    │ remote_head─┼──┐     │        │◀┘
      ...          ├─────────────┤  │     │  next──┼─┐
┌─────────────┐    │ page 3      │  │     ├────────┤ │
│ shard n     │    └─────────────┘  │     │XXXXXXXX│ │
└─────────────┘          ...        │     ├────────┤ │
                   ┌─────────────┐  │     │XXXXXXXX│ │
                   │ page n      │  │     ├────────┤ │
                   └─────────────┘  │     │        │◀┘
                                    └────▶│  next──┼───▶  ...
                                          ├────────┤
                                          │XXXXXXXX│
                                          └────────┘
```
The size of the first page in a shard is always a power of two, and every subsequent page added after the first is twice as large as the page that preceeds it.

```
pg.
┌───┐   ┌─┬─┐
│ 0 │───▶ │ │
├───┤   ├─┼─┼─┬─┐
│ 1 │───▶ │ │ │ │
├───┤   ├─┼─┼─┼─┼─┬─┬─┬─┐
│ 2 │───▶ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │
├───┤   ├─┼─┼─┼─┼─┼─┼─┼─┼─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┬─┐
│ 3 │───▶ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │
└───┘   └─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┴─┘
```
When searching for a free slot, the smallest page is searched first, and if it is full, the search proceeds to the next page until either a free slot is found or all available pages have been searched. If all available pages have been searched and the maximum number of pages has not yet been reached, a new page is then allocated.

Since every page is twice as large as the previous page, and all page sizes are powers of two, we can determine the page index that contains a given address by shifting the address down by the smallest page size and looking at how many twos places necessary to represent that number, telling us what power of two page size it fits inside of. We can determine the number of twos places by counting the number of leading zeros (unused twos places) in the number’s binary representation, and subtracting that count from the total number of bits in a word.

The formula for determining the page number that contains an offset is thus:

where `WIDTH` is the number of bits in a `usize`, and `INDEX_SHIFT` is
